synopsis: Exposure is the opportunity for an event to occur—measured in operating hours, distance, cycles or close approaches—and supplies the denominator needed to convert counts into rates; the accident sources examined lack these denominators, preventing reliable collision-rate comparisons between countries or machine types [f11606, f11610]. Field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance: RAND's 2016 on-road analysis required hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles and tens to hundreds of fleet-years, while off-road machines accumulate less exposure per unit [f313, f5466, f6924, f11613]. Statistical acceleration can reduce exposure by orders of magnitude, but these reductions are not product safety sign-offs, and their transfer to off-road work is limited by missing exposure distributions and disagreement over how accurately open-ended interactions can be modelled [f1945, f1219, f352, f7439]. The booklet recommends logging the existing warning fleet through winter 2026–2027 to build a real-site exposure model; customer telematics, warning logs and site studies are the identified data routes, although the proposed campaign identifies warning logs alone as its source of real exposure and false-alarm data [f708, f6919, f7368, f11615]. Operator acceptance should be assessed through unwanted warnings or interventions per task-specific hour, cycle, reverse maneuver or legitimate close approach, not merely per detection; the only identified field study with a clean denominator was small, reporting alarms in 94% of 618 reverse movements over seven days [f11608, f11609, f11611]. The field exposure needed to substantiate rare missed detections or unintended braking remains uncertain, and the booklet recommends delaying brake control while retaining validated warnings if the safety case remains incomplete [f8181, f10998].
